Data Profiling

data-profiling.Rmd

Profiling makes data transparent and auditable

A governed dataset should not ask you to take its quality on faith. Profiling is the measured description of every column — how complete it is, how it is distributed, where the surprises are — computed from the values themselves and stored in the DGF. Because the profile travels with the governance file, anyone can audit what the data actually looked like, without re-reading the raw file.

create_dgf() profiles every column as it builds the DGF; update_dgf() recomputes the profile for any column whose data has changed.

Universal quality metrics — measured for every column

Regardless of type, each column reports a small set of integrity counts, each as a count and a percentage, and — importantly — only when it occurs, so the profile never pads itself with zeros that would bury the real signal:

  • Distinct — how many unique values (the first clue to whether a column is an identifier, a category, or a measurement).
  • Missing / NA and Missing / Empty — absent values, separating true NA from empty strings, because the distinction often matters.
  • Zero — exact zeros (meaningful for counts, rates, and money).
  • Infinite — non-finite values that signal a computation or import problem.
  • Duplicated — repeated rows/values, surfaced rather than hidden.

Read together these are a quick integrity check: a column that is 40% missing, or one that is all distinct, tells you something before you plot anything.

Type-specific indicators

On top of the universal counts, each type adds the indicators that are meaningful for it:

  • Numeric — the quantile ladder (minimum, Q05, Q25, median, Q75, Q95, maximum) plus mean, skew, and kurtosis, so a skewed or heavy-tailed distribution is visible as a number, not just a picture.
  • Categorical — the level frequencies, ranked, with the long tail capped so the table stays legible.
  • Temporal — the grain (year, month, day, …) and coverage of the range.
  • Text — length and sampled values.

The point of type-specific profiling is that a quality problem looks different for each type: for a number it is an outlier or a skew; for a category it is a rare level or a near-constant column; for a date it is a gap in coverage.

A profile, measured

Build a DGF from the demo dataset and read two real profiles back out — the universal quality counts for any column, and the numeric statistics table:

library(datagoodr)
dgf <- create_dgf(dg_demo, file = tempfile("dgf"), open = FALSE)
dg_properties(dgf, "revenue")   # universal: distinct, missing, zeros, ...

PROPERTIES:

STAT VAL PER
Rows 60
Distinct 60 (100.0%) 
dg_stats(dgf, "revenue")        # type-specific: the numeric statistics

STATS:

STAT VAL
Minimum 55.91
Median 338.8
Mean 534.83
Maximum 2,100.88
Skew 1.44
Kurtosis 1.58

These tables are exactly what the Research Guide renders, read straight from the DGF’s stored profile — no re-reading of the raw data.

How the DGF logs and stores profiles

Each column’s profile is written into the DGF’s rg_* columns and kept as JSON text:

  • rg_properties — the universal counts and type indicators;
  • rg_stats — the statistics tables (quantiles, frequencies);
  • rg_preview — a sample of values;
  • rg_graphics — the data a type’s visual is drawn from;
  • rg_max_chr — the widest value, for layout.

Storing them as JSON (not nested R objects) is deliberate: it survives the .xlsx round trip that a nested column would not, so the profile is portable and the raw data is no longer needed to render the guide. When you re-profile with update_dgf(), only the changed columns’ rg_* cells are rewritten; curated dictionary text is left untouched.

Note. Today’s universal metrics are the integrity counts above. Richer summaries of spread and balance — such as an entropy or concentration measure for categoricals — are under consideration as additional universal indicators.
